chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
title: George Wettling's last days in hospital
summary: Freeman visits the dying Wettling, jokes about 'critical', and recalls he said he no longer had to carry drums.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Anyway, to get back to George, George was a very good painter and did some marvelous things. He would have gone on, I think, as Pee Wee Russell did, and we will talk about that later, to become a fairly good painter, but time was running out on him. He didn't take very good care of his health, and at the end, I went to see him -- his wife called and told me he was in the hospital --

Helen. I went down to the hospital to see George and he was under sedation and he looked terribly thin and I remember going out to get him some magazines, and he wasn't drinking of course, but he liked chocolates and I got him some cigarettes and when I was out, I called up his wife and I said, 'Jean' -- you said Helen, but her name was Jean.

And I just remembered that now. I said, 'Jean, I am terribly sorry to tell you this, but you should know, George is dying, and I doubt very much that he'll live the week out.' Well, as it turned out, I am sorry to say, George died three days later in the hospital.
But, I remember saying one thing to him and it broke him up, made him laugh, I said, 'George, I think

you are going to be okay, because I just heard the doctor say you were merely critical, and that broke him up. He laughed and then I told him -- 'Oh, yes, George, how do you feel being here in the hospital?' He said, 'Well, you know, Bud, it's not really bad at all,' he said, 'And furthermore, I don't have to carry those damn drums around any more.'

So you see, he was going out not really suffering. I think they had given him -- put him under sedation to take the pain away. I don't know just -- I think he might have had cancer of the throat or something like that, I am not sure. But he died laughing.
He was a very lovable guy.
He was a lovable man, but when he got drunk he was -- in a schizoid way, so to speak, he was another person.
One thing I loved very much about George, do you remember that he was tremendously devoted to his terrier, his fox terrier.
Oh, yes, and then of course, he had the cats he adored so much. The day one of them died he was so sad.
But I loved playing with George and of course, those Trio records speak for his marvelous talent, and --
